title: Where Folio stands
lede: Nothing in how Folio writes a course changes in this release. It sets down the state the work of the last weeks has reached, with the numbers it was measured at, so that what comes next can be compared against it. It is not yet where a 0.1 should be, and the last section says why.

sections.heading: Where a lesson stands
sections.body: Sixteen university courses were written afresh and the first two lessons of each were read by independent readers who did not know the version: thirty-two lessons. Fourteen had nothing a teacher would trip over in class. Eleven faults that would stop a lesson were counted across the other lessons: three of time, eight where two materials disagree, none of a wrong answer key or a missing piece. The same reading two releases back counted nine, and one release back twenty-one; that release was repaired within the day.

image.alt: Three readings of thirty-two fresh lessons. Faults that stop a lesson: 9, 21, 11. Lessons with nothing to trip over: 12, 6, 14. Notes from Folio that were true and false: 5 and 5, 3 and 8, 6 and 2

sections.heading: What is checked by a program
sections.body: Numbers in quizzes, graded work and sheet keys are worked out by a program and a wrong one is put right. Python and R that a lesson gives students is run as a student runs it. What a segment asks of students is counted against its minutes. Each lesson opens with a list of what was checked and what is yours to check. On a paid run of two lessons with every material, a lesson cost 65 to 84 cents at the providers’ prices and no answer came back in the wrong shape.

sections.heading: What is not solved
sections.body: Seven of the eight disagreements are of one kind: the running of a graded piece told differently by its brief, its key, the plan and the lesson next to it. Who leads today, whether it is scored alone or in pairs, when it is collected. A reading of six lessons in a row found the same across weeks: one weekly worksheet scored out of 12 in some weeks and 16 in others, a midterm’s rules told two ways. A course written twice from one brief can come out with a different number of lessons. Two kinds of note from Folio are still wrong too often. These are what the next releases are for.

title: One exercise, one version
lede: A reading of thirty-two fresh lessons found the last release worse than the one before it: the same practice stood in two versions in nine lessons, and a mark meant for a chapter number had broken links. This release repairs what that reading found.

sections.heading: A practice on a sheet is shown from the sheet
sections.body: The last release let a plan list what a segment puts on the screen. Where the segment also handed out a worksheet, the plan listed the items one way and the sheet’s writer wrote them another; the slides followed the plan and the key followed the sheet. A segment whose work is set on a sheet no longer carries a list of its own: the slides take the items from the sheet. A list stands where there is no sheet, or where the sheet is only read from.

image.alt: Before: a slide with items A, B, C and a worksheet with items A, D, E for the same practice. After: the slide and the worksheet carry the same three items

sections.heading: “(to confirm)” stays out of links and code
sections.body: The mark after a chapter or page number you did not give was also written inside web addresses and file names, and thirteen lessons had links that no longer opened. An address is now never marked, nor anything inside code or a link; addresses you did not give are still listed for you at the top of the lesson. That list names whose chapter it is (“OpenStax Statistics, ch. 3”) and no longer runs words together.

sections.heading: Fewer false notes on answer keys
sections.body: All five notes the key check left in that reading were wrong. It read “1,046” as two numbers, took the right side of “Then 80 = 5P” for a value to compare, matched a pair of numbers to two choices at once, and could not read a vector written −ȷ for −1. Each is fixed where the check reads the key.

sections.heading: A term-long brief is not timed by the day it is handed out
sections.body: Seminar leadership, taken a group at a time over the term, was said to ask too much for the ten minutes in which its brief is given out. A piece taken over the term is no longer measured against one lesson’s minutes. Hands raised to open a discussion are no longer counted as a vote.

title: What was checked, what is yours to check
lede: With few notes left on a lesson, no note had started to look like no problem. Folio knew which answers a program had worked out and which it never reached, which chapters you gave and which it guessed, and said none of it. Now it does, at the top of every lesson.

sections.heading: A list at the top of each lesson
sections.body: Five lines at most, made from what the lesson holds and not from another reading of it by a model: how many answers and sheet keys a program worked out (and which key it corrected), which it could not reach, which chapters, pages and addresses are not in your brief or files, and how many notes Folio left. It says what was done, never that something is correct. A key you change by hand goes back to unchecked.

image.alt: The list at the top of a lesson: one note, one sheet key no program worked out, two references to confirm; and, folded below, seven answers and two sheet keys a program worked out, one of them corrected

sections.heading: What is on the screen is said once
sections.body: Slides were written from the plan’s prose and had to guess what belonged on the screen; most of the disagreements between a deck and its plan came from there. A plan’s segment can now list what students see, each item in full: a question with its choices, a prompt, a table’s rows. The slides take those items in the plan’s words, and a deck that leaves one out is asked for once more. Code that is typed and run in front of the class is not a slide’s to carry.

sections.heading: Short practices are counted as they run
sections.body: The last release counted every segment by what it asks, and five short practices still ran four to six minutes over. The count had taken “three decisions, each with a reason” as three one-minute answers, six costs worked out from a table as six, and three groups reporting as three things heard. An answer that is calculated or reasoned is now two minutes, and a group’s report two.

sections.heading: What a course will cost, before you write it
sections.body: The estimate shown before writing was a third of the truth: it came from a count of characters that left out the models’ thinking, and from before the checks added since. It now uses what each part cost on paid runs, 66 to 73 cents a lesson with every material, and with your own key you see it in dollars before anything is written. With Folio credits the same lesson is about 200 credits, so the 750 free credits cover about three lessons, where this page used to say eighteen.

sections.heading: Two faults put right
sections.body: Leaving a lesson page could bring up “Something went wrong” in current browsers, where a scroll returns a promise that the page handed on by mistake. And a sheet’s code now uses the names of the lesson’s own data, with a blank where a student puts theirs; a table typed over several lines is run as one statement, not line by line.

title: Keys that are computed, names that hold, chapters that own up
lede: The last release said what was next: a number in a key worked out wrongly, sometimes the same wrong number twice. This one starts on what a teacher has to be able to trust without rereading everything.

sections.heading: The keys to your sheets are worked out by a program
sections.body: A sheet’s answer key had no check of its numbers. Asked to look again, a writer makes the same slip: three separate writings of one calculus lesson all gave e^0.01 where the table wanted (e^0.01 − 1)/0.01. Now a second writer says how each number in a key is worked out from the sheet, a program works it out, and a key that disagrees is corrected and kept only if it then holds; the same number in the plan’s notes is corrected with it. Tried on the 101 keys of 32 lessons, it reached half of them, put right the two that were wrong and raised no false alarm. The other half are not yet reached, and nothing is claimed for them.

image.alt: A worksheet key whose value for h = 0.01 is e to the 0.01 itself; a program works out (exp(0.01) − 1) / 0.01 = 1.00502 and the key and the plan’s notes are corrected

sections.heading: A piece of work has one name
sections.body: Each assignment used to be named by its own writer, often after the next lesson’s plan had already told students to hand it in. Its name is now settled before a word of it is written: what it counts toward, with the lesson’s title when the course has several of the kind. The lesson that sets it, the piece and its rubric, and the lesson that collects it all use that name.

sections.heading: A chapter you did not give says so
sections.body: When your brief names a book but not its chapters, Folio suggests them, and of the ones our readers looked up about half were wrong. In the readings, the sheets, the slides and everything else students are handed, a chapter, section, page range or web address that is not in your brief or your files now reads “ch. 7 (to confirm)”. The number stays, since you can confirm it in seconds; the mark tells a student it is not yet your word. On 32 lessons, half had at least one.

sections.heading: What is the same at every meeting is told to every writer
sections.body: A brief said Java 21 in IntelliJ and four lessons wrote “a terminal and a text editor”; one lesson told students to bring a calculator to a quiz the next lesson forbade it in. Folio now copies out of your brief what holds at every meeting (the size of the class, how it is grouped, the software and its version, what students have, what is not allowed) and gives it to every writer as what no material may contradict.

sections.heading: Three more false notes gone
sections.body: A lab that runs across three segments is measured against all of them, not the longest; a finding that rested on one of Folio’s own instructions and not on your brief is no longer passed to you; and a note about in-class work says which minutes it means.

title: Lessons that fit their minutes, and notes you can act on
lede: Four days of reading whole lessons blind, the way a teacher would the night before, and changing one thing at a time. This release holds what the readers preferred when they saw both versions side by side. It does not hold a claim we could not show: the number of lessons with something that stops the class is about what it was.

sections.heading: Every segment is counted by what it asks
sections.body: A plan’s minutes always added up to the meeting, and a segment could still ask for more than its minutes hold: three problems with working, compared in pairs, three answers heard, in nine minutes. Now what each segment has students do is counted (a short answer, a worked one, a paragraph, a drawing, a turn with a partner, a group heard, a vote), the minutes are added up at fixed rates, and a segment more than a quarter over is trimmed before anything is written from it. The plan’s minutes never change. If it is less than half over, every item stays and each asks less; a practice is never left with fewer than three items, and a discussion keeps its questions, its rounds and its close. Sheets are counted the same way, by their answer rooms and the cells of their tables. Readers who saw the plans with and without this preferred the counted ones for fit in 10 lessons to 3, for substance in 17 to 9, and overall in 18 to 8, of 32.

image.alt: A nine-minute practice as first written, whose parts come to thirteen minutes, and the same practice as it reaches the teacher: every problem kept, each asking less, about nine minutes

sections.heading: When a sheet changes, what is written from it follows
sections.body: A sheet shortened to fit its minutes used to leave the plan’s notes and the slides telling of the longer one: four items on paper, six on the screen, answers read aloud to items nobody had. Now the plan’s account of that segment is written again from the sheet as it stands, notes included, and the slides, study guide and work written afterwards take a sheet’s items from the sheet. Places where sheet, plan and slides disagreed fell from 34 to 26 in one reading of 32 lessons, and from 21 to 9 in another once plans were read again.

sections.heading: Fewer notes, and each one says what is the matter
sections.body: On 32 lessons Folio used to leave ten notes for the teacher, nine of them false alarms. It now leaves two to five. The answer check no longer blames a right key for the way it is written (a quotient, an expression like (ln 9 − 2)/4, a choice that is a command, code on two lines), a line a sheet gives students to repair is not reported as broken, and what is left is said in plain words: where it is, what was worked out, what the text has. A note Folio tried to put right and could not begins “Folio could not fix this itself” and comes first. Keys no longer carry their writer’s remarks about itself.

sections.heading: Slides, study guides, FAQ and discussion prompts are thought over
sections.body: These four are now written with more thinking. Readers given both versions of 16 lessons preferred the new one in 13, and help that would mislead a student was halved. It did not reduce the places where a slide and the plan disagree, which come from materials being written apart.

sections.heading: What a lesson costs, counted honestly
sections.body: Our own figure had been 40 to 46 cents a lesson. It was estimated from the length of the text and left out the model’s thinking. Measured on the providers’ own bills, a lesson of this release costs about 60 cents (one course of a lecture and a lab, two lessons). The same measurement found five kinds of answer that were being refused for a detail and paid for twice, a quiz and a two-meeting plan on every lesson among them; they are read at the first asking now.

sections.heading: What did not change
sections.body: About one lesson in three still has something a teacher would have to fix before class. The kinds have moved: sheets that overran and graded questions only the teacher could see are gone, and what remains is mostly a recurring piece of class work whose schedule the lessons disagree on, and a number in a key worked out wrongly, sometimes the same wrong number twice. Those are next: the first needs the course’s structure decided once and placed by rule, the second needs keys computed, not reread.

title: Three faults at the start of a course
lede: Three things went wrong before a single lesson was written. Each was found by building the same courses several times over and comparing what came out.

sections.heading: “One lesson per lecture” is not a course of one lesson
sections.body: When Folio asks what a lesson should be and you answer “one lesson per lecture” or “one a week”, that says what a lesson is, not how many there are. It was sometimes read as a count, and a fifteen-week course came back as a single lesson. An answer like that now sets the kind of lesson, and the number comes from your weeks and meetings.

image.alt: A brief for a 15-week semester of three lectures a week and the answer “one lesson per lecture”: before, a course of 1 lesson; now, 45 lessons, one for each lecture

sections.heading: Every graded piece has a lesson that holds it
sections.body: An outline could list a final exam at 25% in the grading and then give it to no lesson, so nothing was ever written for it. The outline is now checked against its own grading, and asked once more for any graded piece no lesson holds.

sections.heading: One missing R package no longer stops the rest
sections.body: Before a lesson’s R is run, the packages it loads are fetched. They were fetched together, so one package we do not hold made the whole request fail, and a sheet that only needed the tidyverse was reported as not running. They are now fetched one at a time: what we hold is loaded, and only the line that needs the missing package is reported.

title: R is run before a lesson reaches you
lede: The last release asked the writers to keep to what can be known without running R. That moved the faults; it did not end them. So Folio now runs the R it gives your students, the way it already ran Python.

sections.heading: Every sheet and every piece of work, line by line
sections.body: When a lesson with R is written, each handout and each assignment is run one line at a time in a fresh R session, in a folder that holds the files earlier lessons made (the data file you prepared in week 1 is there in week 2). A line that stops is sent back once to be corrected, and the correction is kept only if the sheet then runs. What still stops is noted on the lesson with R’s own message, so you see exactly which line and why. A line you give students as broken on purpose, to find and fix, is left alone. Tried on courses built before this release, it found the faults our readers had found by hand: a table that was never loaded, a first line that changed to a folder no student has, a plot drawn before its library was loaded.

image.alt: A lab sheet as first written, with two lines that stop and R’s messages beside them, and the same sheet as it reaches the teacher, where every line runs

sections.heading: Where it runs
sections.body: R runs in your browser, in a frame of its own that has no access to your account or your courses and can reach only the folder on our site that holds R itself. It is fetched the first time a lesson with R is written (R and the tidyverse are about 80 MB, kept by your browser afterwards), and not at all for courses without R. On a phone, lessons are kept as written.

sections.heading: What it does not do yet
sections.body: Running finds lines that stop. It does not yet check that an answer key agrees with what R prints; the answer check still works those in Python.

title: Code that runs as it is given, and readings with a name
lede: Folio runs the Python it writes before a lesson reaches you. It cannot yet run R, and the statistics courses showed it: a histogram asked for twice with the same bins, a lab step that used a table nobody had loaded. Until R can be run too, this release makes the writers hold to what can be known without running.

sections.heading: Every sheet stands on its own
sections.body: Code on a handout or in an assignment is now written to run in a fresh session: it loads or creates everything it uses, writes out every setting its result depends on, and names no folder on anyone’s machine. A strict reader traced thirteen R sheets and assignments in two statistics courses step by step afterwards; each loaded what it used and asked students only for what its output shows. Two faults of this kind still got through in a later reading (a fixed folder path, and a key that described a data set as it is generally known and not the file students were given), which is why running R for real is next on our list.

image.alt: A lab sheet before: it uses a table loaded last week and relies on default bins. After: it reads its file, sets its bins and can be run on its own

sections.heading: What to read, in writing
sections.body: The last slide of a meeting that sets work or reading now says what is due and what to read, by name. An assigned reading is never left as “the reader’s chapter”: students get an author and a title. A brief or rubric from an earlier lesson is reprinted as it was, never written again.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: The answer check now looks at every result on a long line of a key, not just the first few, and reads a debt written as −$24.

title: Work done in class fits its minutes, and is written once
lede: We kept rereading the eight first-year courses Folio was never tuned on, fixing what the readers found where it started and building the courses again. At 0.0.26 they found ten faults that would stop a lesson being taught as written. In the most recent reading of each course they found none.

sections.heading: Graded work in class is sized to the time
sections.body: A fifteen-minute group worksheet came with four parts, three tables, two drawings and a paragraph. Telling the writer to size it did not help, so Folio now measures it: work done in class is compared with the minutes its plan gives it and written again, shorter, when it is too much. A sheet that says “work for 20 minutes” in a 13-minute segment is caught the same way.

image.alt: Faults that would stop a lesson, in sixteen lessons of eight new courses: 10 at version 0.0.26, 4 after 0.0.28, 0 at 0.0.29

sections.heading: One version of each graded piece
sections.body: A graded worksheet used to appear twice, once among the handouts with six tasks and once as the graded piece with four and a rubric for the four. The handout writer is now told which pieces are graded and leaves them alone. A lab held every week is a new lab each week, never the first week’s again. A quiz of questions with one right answer is scored by its answers and has no rubric. A later lesson that reuses a rubric is told what the rubric scores and shows it to students again.

sections.heading: Turns students prepare
sections.body: The first student to lead a graded seminar used to see the brief minutes before being scored on it. The first meeting that runs such a piece now gives out the brief, has the teacher model a turn that is not scored, and settles who goes first; scoring begins the meeting after. A step toward a project is written knowing the project as it was set, and a weekly pre-lab entry comes with the procedure it is about.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: A wrong number on a worksheet that its answer key noticed is corrected on the worksheet, not just mentioned to the teacher. A text the plan puts on the screen is on a slide. A character of code keeps its straight quotes. The answer check no longer doubts a right key because a number was spelled out, a sign stood apart from its number, or a fraction was negative, and what it finds wrong in the explanation of a wrong choice it now puts right.

title: No problem is set twice in a week
lede: After the last release we reread the physics, calculus and chemistry courses with strict readers. Nothing blocked a lesson from being taught, and every number was right. What they did find is fixed here.

sections.heading: The quiz, the homework and the recitation work no longer share problems
sections.body: These were each written from the lesson plan alone, so they reached for the same example. A graded problem-set question was the recitation’s own, whose solutions are posted after class, and a graded quiz repeated the practice questions. They are now written in order, the practice quiz first, and each piece is shown what the lesson already sets and told to give other problems.

image.alt: Before: the practice quiz, recitation and problem set all asked for 54 km/h in metres per second. Now each asks a different conversion

sections.heading: Work done before class is about that class
sections.body: When your brief says students take a reading quiz before each lecture, the quiz is now written on the reading for the lecture it is due at, in questions with one right answer. Before, it was on the lecture just given. Work your brief says is done online is handed in online, and no longer collected in class.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: In a week of several meetings, a deadline names the first meeting of the next week, since “next time” could mean tomorrow’s lecture, and slide notes set homework in the meeting where the plan does. A short quiz paper is sized to its minutes. Written work done in class is scored after class, and discussion prompts are questions for students, never notes to the teacher.

title: A week with three lectures and a recitation is planned as one
lede: We built eight common first-year courses Folio had never been tuned on (calculus, chemistry, physics, biology, sociology, composition, Java, accounting) and had strict readers go through two lessons of each. Every number, key and program output they recomputed was right. What they found instead was about how courses meet, and this release fixes it where it starts.

sections.heading: Every meeting of the week gets its plan
sections.body: A course described as “three 50-minute lectures and one 50-minute recitation a week” was planned as a single 50 minutes a week: Folio kept at most three meetings, lost the recitation, and then took the week for one lecture. A lesson now holds up to four meetings, and when you plan a lesson a week, it takes every meeting the week has, whether they are of one kind or several. The physics and calculus courses that showed the problem now come out as 200 minutes a week, each lecture and the recitation with its own steps.

image.alt: Before: one 50-minute lecture planned and three meetings left out. Now: three lectures and a recitation, 200 minutes, each with its plan

sections.heading: Graded clicker rounds and recitation problems have their questions
sections.body: Work that is graded in class every time, such as clicker questions or recitation problems, has one set of instructions and one rubric for the whole term. So the instructions named no questions, and the lesson plan, told the piece was written elsewhere, wrote none either. The plan now writes that day’s questions, with their answers in the teacher’s notes.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: Slides no longer carry notes meant for the teacher, and code on a slide is typed as it runs. A study guide gives again the program or example it talks about, since students do not hold the teacher’s notes. The answer check no longer doubts a right key because of how a number was written (82.0 against 82.0000, or 6.3 × 10⁻⁴).

title: One writer for the worksheet, another for its key
lede: We went on testing writers, one part of a lesson at a time, on the same sixteen university lessons and judged blind. The same thing came out four times: Claude Sonnet writes the better teaching, and GPT-6.1 Sol gets the answers right. This release puts each where it is best for worksheets, as the last did for quizzes.

sections.heading: The key is written from the finished worksheet
sections.body: Judges preferred Sonnet’s worksheets to Sol’s in eleven lessons of sixteen: more to do, better laid out. But Sonnet’s keys to them had wrong answers, a mean said to be above seven of eight patients when it is above six, a bound on copying that its own example breaks. So the worksheet is still Sonnet’s, and its key is now written afterwards by Sol, from the sheet as it stands, every answer worked. On the same sheets, Sol’s keys had no wrong answer and one question left unkeyed; Sonnet’s had four and six. Judges would rather mark from Sol’s key in twelve lessons, from Sonnet’s in none.

image.alt: Left: judges preferred Sonnet’s worksheets in 11 lessons and Sol’s in 4. Right: on the same sheets, Sonnet’s keys had 4 wrong answers and Sol’s had none

sections.heading: What stays as it was, and why
sections.body: We ran the same test on lesson plans and on slides, study guides, FAQ and discussion prompts. Sol was cheaper each time and made fewer slips, and each time the judges chose Sonnet’s: in fifteen lessons of sixteen for plans, eleven for the rest. They found Sol’s thinner, with less for students to think about. So those stay with Sonnet. One thing the test showed against Sonnet is fixed here: its slides tended to show the answer to something the plan had students predict first.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body: About two cents more a lesson, for a key a teaching assistant can mark from. A lesson with every material is now about 40 credits, and the free credits cover about 18 lessons; both are corrected where Folio states them.

title: Quizzes and graded work have a new writer: one wrong key where there were seventeen
lede: The last release ended by saying that rules had stopped helping. So we stopped adding rules and tested the writers instead. On the same sixteen university lessons, with the same plans and worksheets, we had the quiz and the graded work written again by four different writers and judged blind, twice. The writer Folio had been using for them was the worst of the four.

sections.heading: What was measured
sections.body: Each judge saw one lesson and four versions of its quiz and graded work, without knowing who wrote which, worked every key and answer, and counted what was false. GPT-6 Luna, which Folio had used because it was a tenth the price and read as well, had 17 wrong keys or explanations in 32 lessons, and 12 lessons with nothing wrong at all. GPT-6.1 Sol had 1 and 25. Claude Sonnet, which writes the plans, cost more than Sol and came between them. Asking Sol to think longer changed nothing; letting Luna keep the quiz and giving Sol only the graded work gave part of the gain back.

image.alt: Wrong keys or explanations per sixteen lessons: GPT-6 Luna at high effort 8.5, Claude Sonnet at medium 5, GPT-6.1 Sol at low 0.5

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body: About six cents more a lesson. A lesson with every material now uses about 38 credits where we said 32, and the free credits cover about 19 lessons, not 23; both numbers are corrected where Folio states them. We think a key a teacher can grade from is worth six cents.

sections.heading: What we tried and kept as it was
sections.body: The same test on lesson plans went the other way. Sol’s plans cost half as much and had fewer wrong numbers, but the judges preferred Sonnet’s in fifteen lessons of sixteen: more concrete, more for students to do, more of a lesson. Plans stay with Sonnet. The two results fit together: one writer designs the teaching, another writes the items that have to be exactly right.

title: A second pass over the same sixteen lessons: smaller repairs, and where rules stop helping
lede: We wrote the sixteen university lessons again with 0.0.23 and had them read the same way. They had fifteen faults that would stop a class, the same as before this release’s changes, and the five online weeks had six. So this release does not move that number, and we say so. It fixes what the readers named that a rule or a check can settle, and it takes back one mistake of our own.

sections.heading: A question for the whole class is on a slide
sections.body: Twice running, a microeconomics lecture graded its clicker questions and showed none of them: the slide said “Clicker questions: answer alone first”, and the questions with their choices were in the teacher’s notes. Every question a plan puts to the whole class now has a slide of its own, with its choices. A supply-and-demand graph is no longer drawn as a chart, since a chart can only set price along the bottom, the very mistake the lesson warns students about; its points go to the teacher to draw.

image.alt: Left, the slide as it was: clicker questions, answer alone first, with the questions only in the teacher’s notes. Right, a slide for one question: a frost hits the coffee crop, what happens to the price of coffee, with four choices

sections.heading: A number the plan got wrong is corrected in the plan
sections.body: The writer of a lesson’s worksheets works every answer, which makes it the second to compute the plan’s numbers. When they disagreed, the worksheet’s key said “correction to the plan: the standard deviation is about 25.79, not 25.70”, and the plan, its slides and the study guide went on saying 25.70. The correction is now made in the plan before anything else is written from it.

sections.heading: Before the next lesson
sections.body: A test held next time is announced the lesson before, with what it covers, also when it is held beside other work; a midterm had opened a class nobody had told of it. Work graded in class for the first time next lesson is prepared now. A plan sets, hands out and collects only the work its lesson holds, and the lesson’s own quiz is practice, never said to count toward the grade.

sections.heading: Notes to ourselves, taken out
sections.body: Folio’s instructions to its writers came back in the notes a teacher reads: “write no criteria of your own”, “no second set of questions here”, “the handout is written separately”. Sentences that only repeat such an instruction are now removed. And one we caused: in the last few days of work a discussion prompt’s follow-up questions had turned into advice on when to use the prompt. They are questions again.

sections.heading: Two more false alarms
sections.body: The answer check told a teacher that a correct key “does not run” when the key quoted one line of a function, and that four choices all stated the answer because “elastic” is inside “inelastic”. Both are fixed.

sections.heading: What this tells us
sections.body: About one fault a lesson remains, and each new set of lessons brings different ones: a quiz choice that is also right, a key not worked from its own data in R, a lesson that counts on what the one before never asked for. Adding rules has stopped lowering the count. The next work is of another kind: checking a lesson’s graded work against what it actually taught, and writing a course’s arrangements once for all its lessons.

title: The most common university courses, read as a class would meet them: half the faults gone, at the source
lede: We wrote two lessons each of eight courses a university teaches most (microeconomics, a history survey, data structures, intro psychology, an organic lab, research methods, statistics with a lab, biostatistics) and had every lesson read whole, the way a last reader would before class. Thirty things would have stopped a class; fifteen of sixteen lessons had one. Most came from how Folio makes a lesson, not from what a model wrote, so that is where they were fixed. Written again, the same sixteen had fifteen, and seven lessons had none.

sections.heading: Homework that changes every week is written every week
sections.body: Folio writes a weekly response paper once, because its instructions are the same each time. It had come to treat problem sets, lab worksheets and pre-lab quizzes the same way: one text, copied to every lesson. A data structures problem set had no problems in it, a statistics “lab worksheet” asked for two terms from the reading and no R, and a lab’s second quiz was its first, word for word. Thirteen of the thirty faults were this one. Work with its own questions each time is now written for its lesson, from that lesson, and a paper sat in class is never copied.

image.alt: Left, a problem set as it was: complete this assignment to prepare for the reading of the lesson it is due at, with no problem in it. Right, as it is written now: linked-list operations and cost analysis, with its files and steps

sections.heading: One textbook, or none
sections.body: When a brief named no readings, Folio suggested some, a different book for each lesson, and the plans assigned them: a second-year class was to read Knuth for a quiz on Thursday. What Folio suggests is now further reading and nothing in a lesson depends on it. A deadline is given in one wording wherever it is said, the lesson’s own title, where before a paper was due at “the meeting on writing the literature review” in one place and “on developing literature review drafts” in another.

sections.heading: Code keeps its indentation
sections.body: A handout asked which line of a Python function was at fault, with every line set one space in: it could not be read, and it would not run. Folio now asks for each line with its indentation, sends a listing back when it comes squeezed, and the page no longer collapses the spaces inside code, which it had been doing even to listings that were right.

sections.heading: What a lesson relies on is written out
sections.body: A plan said “students describe the histogram on the board” and no slide held a histogram; a graded poll had no choices; a reflection was collected that had no prompt. A plan now writes out a poll’s choices, a prompt and a figure’s numbers, its review looks for them, the slides draw the figure, and a worksheet’s question carries what it needs. The slides, the study guide and the graded work are shown the sheets already written for the lesson, so a slide no longer asks students to write what their sheet prints. The first meeting of a course no longer opens with a quiz on a reading nobody could have been told about.

sections.heading: A key the numbers contradict is corrected, not noted
sections.body: Folio computes the answers its quizzes and keys claim. When one failed, it left a note for the teacher and the wrong key beside it: a median of 4.5 for data whose median is 4. The words at fault are now replaced with what was computed and the item is checked again; only if it still fails does the note remain. Three kinds of false alarm from this check are gone, among them blaming a line of a key for not running on its own.

sections.heading: What we tried and did not turn on
sections.body: We also built a reader that goes over each finished lesson whole and corrects it. On lessons made the old way it found three in four of the known faults. On lessons made the new way it made 63 changes and the count of faults that stop a class did not fall, so it is not part of a build: it costs three credits a lesson and we could not show it earns them. We use it to measure. What remains, about one fault a lesson, is mostly graded work that uses something the lesson did not teach, and that is what we are on now; the first rule for it is in this release and not yet measured.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: The estimate of credits for a lesson rose by two, for the sheets now shown to the slides and the guide; the free credits are said to cover about 23 lessons, where it said 25. A quiz taken in class is given its minutes and comes after what it tests. Quiz explanations say why each wrong choice is wrong.

title: What the checkpoint left wrong: troubleshooting notes are tried, and the teacher’s notes keep up with the page
lede: The checkpoint ended with a list of things still wrong. This release goes down that list. Six weeks written the new way and six the checkpoint’s way were read blind: 8.2 of 10 against 6.9, and for the first time two of the pages were judged ready to release as they stood.

sections.heading: A cause in a troubleshooting note is now tried
sections.body: A note says “if you see this, you did that”, and nobody had done that. In every page we had judged, some cause did not give its symptom. Now each cause that is a mistake in a cell’s code is written out as that cell with the mistake made, and Folio runs it where a student would make it, after the cells before it. A note whose symptom is not what appears goes back to the writer with what did. Our first version of this ran the mistake at the end of the notebook, where later cells had changed the names it used, and four of its six findings were its own errors; we caught that reading them one by one, and it never shipped. Run properly, on six pages it tried 27 causes and questioned two: one rightly (the chart below), one wrongly, over a note that said “near 10” for 9.75, which it now allows.

image.alt: Left, what a note said: no chart appears, make sure the last line of the cell is plt.show(). Right, what Folio ran: the page’s own cell with that line left out; a chart was drawn, and a line of text was printed

sections.heading: The teacher’s notes follow the page
sections.body: When a page was corrected, the notes written for the instructor beside it were not: they went on quoting a number the code no longer printed, or a setting the page had since changed. A fix now carries the instructor’s notes with it, and a guessed number that survives in those notes, or in what a picture is asked to show, is sent back to be corrected. In the blind reading, notes that disagreed with their page fell from ten to two.

sections.heading: The assignment builds on the page
sections.body: A week’s graded work online is the thing the page had students build, handed in with something of their own added. The assignment was written under a rule meant for a classroom (“give new items, not the lesson’s”) and in one case forbade the very notebook its page had told students to submit. It is now told to hand in the page’s work under the page’s names, and in the last runs each assignment names the notebook or the objects it wants.

sections.heading: Corrections that leave no trace, and changes that wait for the writer
sections.body: A correction now takes the place of what it corrects: judged pages had kept “there are two reasons” above three, and a line saying how something had been checked. Leftovers of that kind fell from 21 to 12. And the reader’s ready-made changes are no longer all made on its word: reading 81 of them one by one, nine should not have been made, and every one of the nine wrote something about the course into the page that the page had not given (a 60/40 split, a deadline, a “help forum”). A change that brings in such a thing now goes to the writer, who has the course’s brief and can decline it; the rule catches all nine and two that were sound.

sections.heading: What it costs, and what is still open
sections.body: Two sets of six weeks on the final code cost $0.61 and $0.53 a week; the new check is about a cent and a half of that. Not solved: a cause that is not a mistake in code (an install, a click, the order cells are run in) is still only as true as the writer makes it, and the judged pages still had six false causes in eighty-one. We could not test the screens behind sign-in, a real course being written in the browser, or code run in the browser on the live site; the files that last one needs are all in place and answer. And no teacher has yet read these pages: every score here is another model’s.

title: A question slide keeps its points beside their dots, and a link opened in another tab finds its place
lede: Two more things from the walk through the live site, one of them a correction to the last release’s fix.

sections.heading: Question slides in the editor
sections.body: On a slide laid out as a question, each point was centred on its own line while its dot stayed at the left edge of the slide, a hand’s width away. The points now stand together as one block in the middle, each beside its dot, in the editor as on the slide you show.

image.alt: The slide editor on a slide laid out as a question: the title centred, and under it two points in one centred block, each with its dot directly beside it

sections.heading: A link to a material, opened behind another tab
sections.body: The last release made a link such as “…?m=quiz” open on the quiz. Checking it on the live site, it still opened at the top when the page was loaded in a tab that was not in front, which is how most links get opened: a browser tells a hidden page nothing about its size changing, and that was what the fix listened for. It now watches what is added to the page as well, and goes on looking until the tab has been in front for a moment.

title: A course fits a tablet and a phone when you are signed out, and a link to a quiz opens on the quiz
lede: After the checkpoint we went through the live site in a browser, screen by screen, at the widths of a desktop, a tablet held upright and a phone. Most of it held. Four things did not.

sections.heading: The bar across a course was wider than the screen
sections.body: Signed out, the bar at the top of a course carries a Sign in button, and with it the bar was 46 pixels wider than a phone and 125 wider than a tablet held upright: on the phone the whole page slid sideways, and on the tablet the menu and Sign in sat past the edge where nobody could press them. Our tests did not look at these two screens at these widths. Below a wide screen the bar now shows Sign in as its mark alone and Sources as its icon, search moves into the menu, and a long course title gives way before any button does. The tests now try eight widths.

image.alt: A lesson on a tablet held upright: the bar holds the course title, Overview, Lessons, Materials, the history and sources icons, Export, the menu and the sign-in mark, all on the screen

sections.heading: A lesson has the tablet’s whole width
sections.body: On the same tablet the list of lessons stood beside the lesson and left it a column 368 pixels wide, in which a rubric’s table pushed the page sideways. The list now appears on wide screens only; below that, lessons are reached from the overview and the bar, as on a phone.

sections.heading: A link to one material opens on it
sections.body: Open a quiz from the overview and the address ends in “?m=quiz”. Copied to a colleague, or reloaded, that address opened on the top of the lesson plan: the page looked for the quiz before it had finished filling. It now finds it again as the page fills, and stops as soon as you scroll.

sections.heading: Small things to press
sections.body: On a phone the smallest targets were “Or open a sample course”, the links at the foot of the home page and “Show why” under a question, each about 18 pixels high. They are taller.

title: Checkpoint: where a week stands after a day of taking it apart
lede: This release closes what the last four left open, and marks the place. A week of an online coding course now costs $0.53 to write and check where it cost $0.97 four releases ago, the reading and fixing of a page take about a minute where they took four, and pages read blind by a reviewer score what they did or a little better. What is still wrong is listed at the end.

sections.heading: The reader was policing rules meant for the writer
sections.body: The model that reads a page is told about the course as the writer is, and with it came the writer’s own instructions: how deadlines are to be worded, what is written separately, who lectures. It held pages to them. Nearly half of what it listed was no fault of the page, and some of its ready-made changes wrote a deadline, a grading rule or a demand for one version of Python into a page that had none. It is now told those instructions are not its to enforce. What it lists that is no fault fell from 47 in a hundred to 37, and it lists a third fewer things. On twelve pages with 28 known faults it found 25, where it had found 27 before; so we judged the finished pages rather than the reading: six weeks each way, read blind, 7.75 of 10 against 7.83, two stopping faults against three, nine false statements against eleven.

image.alt: Four bars: what one week of an online coding course cost to write and check. Release 0.0.15, $0.97. Release 0.0.16, $0.68, the page written without thinking itself to a stop. Release 0.0.18, $0.58, the reading at lower effort. Release 0.0.19, $0.53, the reader no longer polices the writer’s rules

sections.heading: Rules that were read out to students
sections.body: Several things Folio tells the writer were turning up on the page as if students needed them: “every component is scored by points or rubric levels, not complete or incomplete”, “nothing is handed out or said aloud”, and parts whose only content was “open the separately posted step”. Each came from an instruction worded so that it asked to be repeated. They are reworded, and in the last runs on five courses none of them appears.

sections.heading: Things that did not agree with each other
sections.body: A page gave a small ungraded step “by Sunday” that the step’s own text set five weeks on: the page is now told each piece’s real deadline. A version check showed the Python that Folio runs code on, above a sentence saying it should print the course’s: such a cell never shows Folio’s versions now, and the setup makes one environment with exactly the versions the course names. An assignment gave other measurements to an object the page had students build under the same name: a new item now has a name of its own. A picture went on being asked to show a number the code no longer printed. And a variable’s name was reused for a function further down, which broke the notebook when run again from the top.

sections.heading: The answer check, measured again
sections.body: After the four repairs of 0.0.16, on the same 113 questions: it finds six of nine real errors where it found five, and blames two of 64 sound questions where it blamed five, for half the money. The measurement also showed that one of the repairs had let an error through, by matching a result of 1.459 to a stray “1” further along the line; that is mended in this release and has a test.

sections.heading: Still wrong
sections.body: A troubleshooting note still sometimes names a cause that does not give the symptom it is listed under; asking the writer for true ones was not enough, and the real answer is to run them. The reader still proposes a change that should not be made about seven times in a hundred. A fix sometimes leaves the corrected sentence beside the one it corrects. The teacher’s summary of what students’ work holds can go stale when a page is mended. The last checks in this release were made with command-line tools, which show what a page says but not what it costs. No teacher has yet read any of these pages: every score here is another model’s.

title: A week’s page is read and put right in half the time, with fewer notes left for you
lede: After a week’s page is written, a second model reads it as a student would and the writer puts right what it finds. That reading and fixing had become more than half of what a week costs. We took it apart, call by call and note by note, and most of what we changed is a fault removed.

sections.heading: What we found in the notes
sections.body: We had twelve first readings checked one by one. Every reading found every fault that mattered, 28 in all. But between a third and a half of what each reading listed was no fault, and the same kinds came back: a checklist’s minutes added up a hundred too many; a deadline or a grading rule written into a page that had never given one; “your version may differ a little” turned into a demand. Small changes of that kind were being made to pages without anyone asking. The reader is now told what is not its to list, and the false totals are gone: none in twelve readings where there had been five.

image.alt: Three figures, each the mean of six weeks. What the reading and the fixes cost: $0.23, where it was $0.34. How long they take: 2 minutes, where it was 4. Notes left for the teacher to settle in a week: 0.3, where it was 1.5

sections.heading: Faults of ours that sent pages back
sections.body: Folio’s own check asked every notebook week for a screenshot of a cell and a recording of it being run, though the cell’s real output is already on the page: eleven weeks of twelve were sent to be mended for pictures a teacher would then have had to make. It no longer asks. A rule about work that depends on a classmate’s was written so that it was pasted, word for word and unreadable, into the checklists of weeks with no such work; it is rewritten. A note that a sentence quoted an old number was sent to the writer even after the reader had already corrected the sentence. A checklist item was left out of the week’s hours if it so much as mentioned the word optional, which put some weeks forty minutes under what they asked. And the teacher’s list of things to check quoted numbers from before the code was run; those entries now go when the run replaces the numbers.

sections.heading: What we tried and did not take
sections.body: The reader now reads at a lower effort, since it no longer has to run the page’s code in its head: it found the same 28 faults, in under half the time. We tried the same economy on the writer’s fixes, and it failed: twelve fixes made without thinking first were set beside the twelve made with it, blind, and lost ten times, once by inventing the output of code that had been run. Fixes think as they did.

sections.heading: The result
sections.body: A week of an online coding course costs about $0.58 to write, where it was $0.68, and is ready about two minutes sooner. Six weeks written each way were read blind: 7.7 of 10 against 7.3, the gain in sentences that should never have been on the page. Two of the six new pages had a fault that would stop a student, both of kinds seen before these changes; one, a version check that showed Folio’s Python and not the course’s, has a fix in this release that is not yet measured.

title: Claude is now told what each part of its answer is for
lede: Looking for what else a week’s page costs, we found something that cost nothing and was simply broken: most of the notes that tell the model what each field of its answer is for were never sent to it. They are now, and pages come out better formed for the same money.

sections.heading: What was lost on the way
sections.body: Folio holds a model to a shape: a page has parts, a part has blocks, a block has a kind, a title, a picture to ask for. Beside most fields is a line saying what belongs there. For Claude, the library that sends the shape dropped that line from every field that has a default or is used twice: 116 of 160, among them what a callout’s title is, what a picture must give a student who cannot see it, and nearly everything about the notes a teacher gets with a week. The model worked from the long instructions alone. Other providers’ models were not affected.

image.alt: Two bars. As it was, 44 of the 160 descriptions written in Folio’s shapes reached Claude. Now all 160 do. Among those that never arrived: what a callout’s title is, what a picture gives a student who cannot see it, who to contact this week and what to say

sections.heading: What changes on the page
sections.body: Six weeks written each way were read blind, and the reader, asked whether the pages fell into two kinds, sorted all twelve correctly. With the descriptions, callouts have titles, the teacher’s notes name this week’s variables and say what to write to a student who has not started, and more pictures are asked for: 7.9 of 10 against 7.5, the difference in form and in the teacher’s notes, not in what is taught. Four lessons taught in a room, read the same way, came out level. The cost is the same.

sections.heading: What we tried and did not take
sections.body: A fifth of what a week’s page costs is empty fields: every block writes ten, and seven are usually blank. Let the model leave them out and it does; but five pages of six then came back as a handful of blocks and the word “Placeholder”. They stay. What is left of a page’s cost is the page.

sections.heading: Still wrong
sections.body: The teacher’s list of things to check in a week with code can quote numbers from before the code was run, which differ from those on the page. The page itself is put right; that list is not yet.

title: A week of an online coding course costs about a third less to write
lede: We traced every call Folio makes for a week of a course and found that a quarter of the money bought nothing: pages written and thrown away. That is gone, and the pages that come out were judged no worse.

sections.heading: Where the money went
sections.body: Before writing a week that teaches code, the model thought at length, working out by hand what every cell would print. In four runs of six it thought until its answer was full, wrote nothing, and was asked again; the second time it thought little and wrote a good page. The page is now written straight away, at the same care as before, and Folio runs the code to learn what it prints, as it has since 0.0.13. A page whose optional reading took no time was also being written again whole for that alone; it no longer is, and an optional item with no time shows none.

image.alt: Two bars. As it was, a week cost $0.97, of which $0.23 was written and thrown away and $0.22 the week’s page. Now it costs $0.68: the page $0.13, putting right what the review found $0.15, the review $0.14, the rest $0.17

sections.heading: How we know the pages are no worse
sections.body: Six weeks written each way, from three courses, were read blind by a reviewer who did not know which was which, as an instructor would before releasing them: 8.1 of 10 for the new way and 7.9 for the old, one page with a fault that would stop a student on each side. A cheaper setting we tried first, which saved a little more, scored 6.9 with four such faults in a reading where the old way scored 8.3, and we did not take it. One thing is not as good: a first draft now draws more notes from its review (about seventeen where there were eleven), so the review and the fixes cost a little more and a teacher is left a note more often. It is counted in the figure above.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: A fix now gives only the blocks that change; it used to type whole parts again, half of them untouched. The answer check costs half what it did for each question, and four faults of its own are mended: it took 2 for 3, could miss an error it had found twice when the two findings quoted the text differently, let a form narrow the rounding rule, and blamed a question for a form left empty. A week with no code, or a lesson taught in a room, costs about what it did; a lesson with a quiz to check, a little less.

sections.heading: What this is measured on
sections.body: Three courses in Python, first weeks, with Folio credits (Claude Sonnet 5.5), and one week of a Unity course, which came out better the new way in its one comparison. With your own key and another model, pages are written as before.

title: A fault of ours in online courses, and four things teachers asked for
lede: First, a correction. For some hours after the last release, a course taught online could not be written with a paid model, and the answer check added two releases ago was not really checking. Both are fixed. Then: slides with tables and charts, a copy of a handout for students still learning English, standards codes on lessons, and slips and cards that print as slips and cards.

sections.heading: What went wrong, and what we changed so it does not again
sections.body: The last release let a week’s page hold tables and notes as real content. The way that was described to the model made the request larger than the model’s provider accepts, and every weekly page of an online course was refused; lessons taught in a room were not affected. Separately, the check that computes answers was asking the model for a form in a way that the paid models answered with an empty one, so it had been passing everything without computing anything. We did not see either because our test runs used a route that does not hold the model to the shape of its answer. Both are fixed, and before each release every such shape is now sent to the provider itself. Run for real on a statistics week, the check computed five of seven answers.

sections.heading: Slides can hold a table or a chart
sections.body: A deck was bullets and nothing else. Where a lesson compares things under the same headings, the slide is now a table; where it compares numbers or follows them over time, a chart drawn from those numbers, bars or a line. In PowerPoint the table is a real table and the chart a real chart, so you can restyle either or change a value there; in Folio you change the numbers under the slide and the chart is drawn again. Numbers made up to show a shape are marked as an illustration on the slide. Diagrams and drawings are not made yet.

image.alt: A slide with a bar chart of two bars, 8 and 2, labelled in milligrams of starch and marked as an illustration, with one question under it

sections.heading: A copy of a handout with language supports
sections.body: About six teachers in ten say they lack materials for students still learning English. Under each handout you can now ask for a copy with supports: the same task, questions and answers, with shorter instructions, a word bank, one worked example and sentence starters. Nothing is made easier or taken out, and nothing on the student’s sheet says it is a different version. It is a draft for you to read: of the first nine we had judged, five could be printed as they were and four needed a line or two changed, usually a word’s meaning.

sections.heading: Standards on the lessons that serve them
sections.body: When your brief or your files name standards by their codes, each lesson now says which it serves, in the plan and in what you export. Folio keeps only codes you gave it and never adds one.

sections.heading: Slips and cards print as slips and cards
sections.body: An exit ticket took a page to itself, and cards came as a list that could not be cut apart. In a document, slips now come three to a page with a line to cut along, and cards one to a cell of a grid.

title: The sheets a lesson hands out are written, not just named
lede: Four changes, each made because teachers say it is where generated lessons fall short: materials a plan names and does not include, pictures left for the teacher to make, quizzes that will not go into the LMS, and lessons that only ask students to repeat what they were shown.

sections.heading: Handouts, written in full
sections.body: A plan would say “hand out the exit ticket” or “students sort the cards”, and that was all there was of the ticket and the cards. Counted over six of Folio’s own courses, a lesson needed about thirteen things made and nearly half were left to you. For a lesson taught in a room, Folio now writes every sheet the plan puts in students’ hands: worksheets, exit tickets, organizers, cards, short texts, each from the plan’s own numbers and examples, with room to answer sized to the question. The answers stand beside the sheet for you and never on it. Sheets are edited under the plan and exported with it, each on its own page. A reviewer who worked all 94 answers on the first twenty sheets by hand found none wrong; nine sheets could be printed as they were, eight needed a small fix and three were not usable, mostly for their layout.

image.alt: A worksheet under a lesson plan: ratio tables with empty cells to fill in, room to write under each, and an answer key for the teacher below the sheet

sections.heading: What the course wrote is shown, not described
sections.body: On an online page, seven picture places in ten asked for a picture of something the page had itself written: your notes as they should now stand, a model email, a filled-in table. You were left to make each by hand from its description. The page now holds the thing itself: real text and real tables, edited where they stand, read aloud properly, and real tables in a Word file. One that shows what students are about to write stays closed until they open it to compare. On the first two courses written this way, a three-week course in technical writing went from about fourteen pictures for you to make to none; in psychology, the ten left are real screens and drawings. Read one by one, 41 of 54 could be used as they were and none was unusable.

image.alt: A page of notes shown as a table on the course page, with a note on one column and a button to hide it again

sections.heading: Quizzes that go into Canvas
sections.body: The quiz bank left Folio as a spreadsheet, to be typed into the LMS again. It can now leave as a package Canvas imports (Settings, Import Course Content, QTI .zip file): one quiz for each lesson, with its key. Canvas marks the questions that have one right choice and the numeric ones; a short answer becomes a question you read, with the model answer as its comment. It imports as Classic Quizzes, the kind teachers report importing reliably. We have checked that the package is well formed and follows the format; we have not yet imported one into a real Canvas course, so please tell us if yours does not come in cleanly.

sections.heading: One task beyond practice, and a quiz as hard as the lesson
sections.body: We measured 40 of Folio’s lessons the way a published study measured machine-written plans. Where that study found 45 activities in 100 asking students only to recall, Folio’s had 9. But in mathematics and chemistry no lesson went beyond practising the method just shown, the teacher explained for up to 28 minutes at a stretch, and the quiz was shallower than the lesson. A plan now holds one task a step beyond practice, at the students’ level (find and fix the mistake, choose between two ways and say why), in place of some of the practice; long explanation is broken by something every student does; and a quiz asks at least once for the hardest thing the lesson did. Measured again on nine lessons: none stops at practice, the longest stretch of explanation is 16 minutes, and students are active for 62 minutes in 100, up from 38.

sections.heading: You can see which answers were checked
sections.body: A quiz question whose key Folio computed, and found to hold, now says so under it. Change the question and the mark goes, since what was checked is no longer what is there.

title: Folio runs the code it writes
lede: The Python on a week’s page is now run before you see the page, and the page shows what the code really prints. Answers that can be worked out are worked out, and the ones that don’t hold are marked for you.

sections.heading: The page shows what the code prints
sections.body: In an online course taught in a notebook, Folio wrote each cell and, under it, what it expected the cell to print. Nothing had run. Now every cell of a week is run in order, in a fresh notebook, and the output on the page is what came out: in place of what was written, or under a cell that had none. A chart a cell draws is placed under the cell. A cell that fails is sent back to be corrected with its real error, and so is a sentence that quotes a number the code does not print; what could not be put right is noted for you. Each output says what ran it. One kind of cell is left as written: one that asks the computer about itself, such as which version of pandas is installed, since the answer is about your students’ computers, not Folio’s.

image.alt: Before, the output under a cell was what the writer expected, here a wrong 5; now it is what the code printed when Folio ran it, 6, marked as run on Python 3.14

sections.heading: Answers that can be computed are
sections.body: The mistakes in a generated course were not where we looked for them. In four courses, the code on the pages was right, but 8 of 49 quiz questions and answer keys had a wrong key or a wrong explanation, and no reading had caught one. For any question or answer key with code or numbers in it, Folio now builds the item’s data, computes what the item claims, and compares the result with the words in the item. What fails twice is marked on the item, with the value it states and the value computed. Folio never changes a key by itself: you decide. On the first two courses written this way it marked three real mistakes in 43 items, among them the one pictured, and one item that was right; what caused that false alarm is fixed.

image.alt: An answer key that gives a chi-square statistic of 0.581, with a note under it: Folio ran this and it did not hold; computed from the counts, it is 0.867

sections.heading: Where the code runs, and what it can reach
sections.body: The code runs in your own browser, so it costs you nothing and needs no account. It is shut in a frame that has none of Folio’s storage and is allowed no connection of any kind: it cannot read your courses or your keys, and it cannot send anything anywhere. A cell that runs too long, or takes too much memory, is stopped. The first time a course needs it, your browser fetches Python and its libraries (about 6 MB, or about 25 MB with pandas and Matplotlib) and keeps them. Folio’s Python is 3.14, with pandas 3.0, NumPy 2.4, Matplotlib 3.10, SciPy 1.18, statsmodels 0.14 and scikit-learn 1.8; a course you write for older versions is still written for yours, and its outputs say which version ran them. On a phone the code is not run, and the page is kept as written.

image.alt: Folio’s page holds your courses, account and keys; the runner is a frame with a Python in it; code goes in, text and pictures come out, and nothing else passes

sections.heading: A notebook of each week
sections.body: When you export a course as a zip, each week that has Python now comes with a Jupyter notebook: the week’s words as text and its code as cells, in order, so a student can run the week instead of typing it out. The teacher’s copy also shows what each cell printed.

sections.heading: Two faults found on the way
sections.body: Checking answers by running them showed that code of more than one line, inside a quiz choice or an answer, had its straight quotes turned into curly ones with the prose around it, and would not run when copied; such code is now left exactly as written. And a security review of this work found that a backup file made by hand could give a file a type the browser would run as a page; a file kept with a course is now shown only as a picture or a video, and anything else is a download. That fix went out earlier today.

title: Work that waits on a classmate is due after theirs
lede: Three faults in how a course is put together, each found by reading a whole course through, and one plain page of what to know before you rely on Folio.

sections.heading: A review is due after the draft it reviews
sections.body: In an online course with peer review, the draft and the reviews of it were both due on Sunday night, so there was nothing to review until the hour the review was due. Work that needs a classmate’s work to exist now comes after it: what classmates will work on is posted by Thursday, and the work on it is due that Sunday, the same every week.

image.alt: Before, a weekly draft and the reviews of it were both due Sunday night; now the draft is posted by Thursday and the reviews are due Sunday

sections.heading: A milestone you name gets a task of its own
sections.body: When a brief named a step on the way to a larger piece, a prospectus in week 8 or a draft in week 10, Folio mentioned it in that week’s summary and wrote no task for it: no length, no contents, nothing to hand in. Each such milestone is now a task in the week you gave, and Folio no longer adds steps of its own that fall due the same day.

sections.heading: A week’s hours are estimated, not made to fit
sections.body: An online week is planned for the hours you give it, and every week came out at exactly that number, including weeks that would take a student half as long again. Each item is now timed from what it asks (reading, a first draft, steps to follow, finding a partner), work that does not fit moves to another week or becomes optional, and the second reader times each item again and says where it disagrees.

sections.heading: What to know before you rely on it
sections.body: The About page now says three things plainly: Folio writes in English for schools and universities in the United States and Canada; what it writes is a draft for you to read before you teach it; and for a course that teaches software, it needs your notes on the version your students use.

title: Your pictures on every device you sign in on
lede: The last release let you put pictures, clips and files into a page, and kept them in the browser you added them in. They now go to your account as well.

sections.heading: Added once, there everywhere
sections.body: When you are signed in, each picture, clip or file you add to a course’s pages is sent to your account after the course itself. On another device, a page that names one fetches it when you open the page, and an export or a backup made there fetches whatever it still lacks. A file can be up to 95 MB and an account can hold 2 GB; anything larger stays in the browser it was added in, and a backup file still carries it. The files are private to your account, and deleting a course or the account deletes them. Nothing changes if you do not sign in: everything stays in your browser, as before.

image.alt: A picture added on this computer is sent once to your account and fetched by your other device when you open the page

title: What a review finds is put right where it stands
lede: We listed what was wrong with how Folio writes a course, then worked through the list and wrote six courses again to see what held: a doctoral seminar, a grade 8 writing unit, and four online courses. This release is what came of it, including two faults of our own that the check-ups turned up.

sections.heading: Problems are mended, not written around
sections.body: Every lesson plan and weekly page is read a second time by another model before anything is built on it. Where that reading found problems it could not fix in a few words, Folio used to write the whole page again and keep whichever version had fewer. The new page lost the problems it was told of and brought its own, so about as many reached you as before. Now only the parts at fault are written again, and the reviewer reads them again, told what the first reading found. Over 34 weekly pages of three online courses, the first reading left 259 notes and 67 were left at the end. That is not none: a reviewer reading a page again usually finds something new, and some of what stays is yours to decide.

image.alt: Before, every part of a page was written again when a review found problems; now only the parts at fault are written again and read again. Across 34 pages, 259 notes became 67

sections.heading: Each note can be fixed, or settled, on its own
sections.body: Notes on a plan used to stand as one paragraph with one button that cleared them all. Each now has its own line, with two choices: “It’s fine”, or “Fix it”, which writes again the part the note is about and leaves the rest of the page, and its pictures, as they are. When a note turns on a choice that is yours (should two things be due the same night?), Folio says so and asks; type what you have decided and it fixes the page to match. A course with notes still on it now says how many on its card in the library, where it used to look finished.

image.alt: A lesson plan with two notes from its review, each with its own Fix it and It’s fine

sections.heading: Weeks are no longer written one at a time
sections.body: A week is written from the weeks before it, so that it uses their names and carries on their work. Each used to wait for the one before to be written, checked and corrected. A week now starts from the one before as first written, while that one is still being checked, and its own check reads the corrected version. A fourteen-week online course that took about three hours to write took about an hour and forty minutes on the same machine, with other courses being written beside it; a thirteen-meeting doctoral seminar took sixteen minutes. We then read all fourteen weeks for a project, scene, script or setting that a later week names wrongly because of this, and found none. What we did find was of another kind: a later week not allowing for what a challenge had added to a shared file. That is on our list.

sections.heading: Pictures, clips and files go into the page
sections.body: A weekly page for a software course asks for screenshots, short recordings and files, and says what each must show. Until now there was nowhere to put them. Each place now takes a file: pick it, drop it on the place, or paste a screenshot. A picture gets a caption and a description for students who cannot see it, both yours to edit. Pictures go into the Word file, everything goes into the zip in a media folder, and a backup file carries them. They are kept in this browser only for now: signing in does not yet carry them to your other devices, and the page says so where it matters.

image.alt: Two places for screenshots on a weekly page, each saying what the picture must show, with an Add picture button, and a file to attach

sections.heading: A picture can be looked at beside its step
sections.body: A review that reads a page’s words cannot see its pictures. When we followed a course by hand, the pictures were where the mistakes hid: a window from a later step, a setting cut off at the edge. “Check” shows the picture to a model together with the steps that lead to it, and lists where the two disagree, and anything in the picture that names a person or an account. We tried it on twenty pictures from that course, ten in their own places and ten swapped for another: all ten swapped ones were named. Of the ten in the right place, five came back clean and the rest with notes that were true of them, such as an outline that had been asked for and not drawn.

image.alt: A screenshot of an Inspector with a note under it: the caption speaks of a setting that the picture cuts off

sections.heading: What Folio could not check is listed for you
sections.body: When a page teaches software, the names of menus and buttons change from one version to the next, and Folio writes from what you gave it and, past that, from memory. We tested whether it could look the names up instead: a model with only the tool’s own documentation got 129 of 244 facts right that we had checked in the tool itself, 13 wrong, and had nothing on the rest. That is not good enough to state as fact, so Folio does not do it. Instead, each week’s instructor notes now list what the page states without a source of yours to go by, for you to try before the week opens; and when a brief names software without a version, Folio asks which.

sections.heading: Two faults of ours, found and fixed
sections.body: Since version 0.0.7 Folio has recorded, for each graded component, whether it is scored or graded complete or incomplete. Writing courses again for this release, we found it had marked nearly every component as complete or incomplete, a 60% seminar paper among them, and told every page so. The question it was asked could be read two ways. It is now asked in words that cannot, and believed only when your brief speaks of completion itself. If you made a course since October 4, look at the grading table on its syllabus and set each component as you mean it. The second: a week’s total hours counted optional reading and make-up work, so a nine-hour week read as ten.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: Later lessons see more of what earlier ones said: the two lessons just before are shown at length, and those further back in brief where they used to be left out. Lines added to a file after it was first written are passed on with it. A weekly task set in the same words every week is written for an online week as that week’s work, not as something handed in at the start of a class. Two different pieces of one component done in class are each written, where the second used to be a copy of the first. A test covers only what was taught before it is sat. An exit ticket in a live session has one standing place. Screenshots are asked for where steps are followed on a screen, not under every list of steps. The grading table shows how many pieces a component has and what each is worth.

title: Later weeks use the names earlier weeks gave
lede: We followed a fourteen-week course by hand, step by step, and looked at every picture in it. Most of what went wrong was not in any one page: it was between pages. This release puts what we learned into how Folio writes, so the next course does not need the same hand.

sections.heading: The files a course has written are passed on whole
